--- title: "Reweighting Floats by Where They Could Have Gone" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 execute: cache: false --- ## The problem in one sentence Floats drift into some places (often warm, convergent water) more than others, so a plain average of their profiles over-counts those places and runs warm. ## The fix in one sentence Weight each profile by **the area it stands in for**. That area is one over how many floats were *expected* to land at its spot, given where every float actually was a few weeks earlier. **The recipe.** For each float: 1. Take its real position a few cycles ago (its **anchor**). 2. Drift a cloud of particles from the anchor through the model currents plus some random noise. The cloud is everywhere the float could plausibly be now. 3. Spread the float's "one expected profile" evenly over its cloud. A cloud covering 10% of the box has density $1/0.10 = 10$. 4. Add up all floats' cloud densities to get the **stacked density**. At each real profile, it is the sum over every cloud the profile falls in. 5. **Weight = 1 / stacked density.** ## Example 1: three floats The clouds here are flat rectangles so the arithmetic is easy. * **A** sits in a jet. The jet keeps it on a narrow track, so its cloud is a thin ribbon covering 1% of the box. Density is $1/0.01 = 100$, so its weight is $1/100 =$ **1% of the box**. * **B** and **C** sit in quiet water. Their clouds are wide, and both cover the *same* 20% of the box. Where they overlap the density is $1/0.2 + 1/0.2 = 10$, so each gets $1/10 =$ **10%**. They split the area they share. ::: {#cell-fig-abc .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Flat clouds (rectangles) and the resulting weights. A's thin jet ribbon earns it 1 percent of the box; B and C share one 20 percent cloud, 10 percent each.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-abc-output-1.png){#fig-abc width=450 height=450} ::: ::: ::: {#5d9baae3 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
float cloud_area density weight
A 0.01 100.0 0.01
B 0.20 10.0 0.10
C 0.20 10.0 0.10
``` ::: ::: If B had been alone, it would have received the full 20%. The weights add to 21%, which is the part of the box the floats can speak for. The remaining 79% is a **gap**, and only a map can fill it. ## Example 2: why this removes the warm bias The south half of the box is warm ($Z=+1$) and the north half cold ($Z=-1$), so the true box mean is $0$. Convergence has collected three floats in the warm half and left one in the cold half. * The three warm floats' clouds each cover the warm half (50%). Stacked density is $3 \times 1/0.5 = 6$, so each gets weight $1/6 \approx 17\%$. **Together they get 50%.** * The lone cold float's cloud covers the cold half. Its density is $1/0.5 = 2$, so it gets **50%** by itself. ::: {#cell-fig-warm .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Three crowded warm floats share the warm half; the lone cold float stands in for the whole cold half.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-warm-output-1.png){#fig-warm width=480 height=450} ::: ::: | | calculation | box mean | |---|---|---| | simple average | $(1+1+1-1)/4$ | \+0\.50 | | reweighted | $3 \times \tfrac16 \times (+1) + \tfrac12 \times (-1)$ | \+0\.00 | | truth | | $0$ | Crowding no longer buys extra influence: three floats in the same place count as one area, not three. ## Example 3: a map, checked by the floats (the "doubly robust" version) Weights alone can only speak for places the clouds reach. A map can fill in everywhere, but maps built from crowded floats lean toward where the floats crowd. The doubly robust version uses both: **draw a map, then let the floats check it.** Same box as Example 2: warm half $+1$, cold half $-1$, truth $0$. **Step 1: draw a map.** Kriging gets the crowded warm half right ($+1$). The cold half has a single float, so the map hedges toward the overall data and says $0$ there instead of $-1$. The map's box average is \+0\.50, which is too warm. **Step 2: check the map at each float.** A float's **residual** is what it measured minus what the map says at its spot. | float | measured | map says | residual | weight | |---|---|---|---|---| | W1, W2, W3 (warm) | $+1$ | $+1$ | $0$ | $\tfrac16$ each | | C1 (cold) | $-1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $\tfrac12$ | Three of the four floats say "the map is fine here". Only the cold float sees the mistake. **Step 3: average the residuals and add that to the map.** | how residuals are averaged | correction | final answer | |---|---|---| | plainly: $(0+0+0-1)/4$ | $-0.25$ | \+0\.25 (still warm) | | with the cloud weights: $3\times\tfrac16\times 0 + \tfrac12\times(-1)$ | $-0.50$ | \+0\.00 ✓ | A plain average of the checks is skewed for the same reason the plain average of heat content was: most checks come from where the map is already right. The weights give the lone cold float the say it deserves, and it reports that the map is off by $-1$ over half the box. **Why it is called "doubly robust": it is right if *either* piece is right.** * **Perfect map:** every residual is $0$, so the correction is $0$ whatever the weights are. * **Perfect weights:** the correction measures the map's error exactly, so even a poor map gets fixed. * **Both a bit off:** the two errors multiply instead of adding. For example, suppose the drift model wrongly gives the cold float only 40% instead of 50%: ::: {#31cbf784 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
method answer (truth = 0)
weights only 0.20
map + check, poor map (cold half = 0) 0.10
map + check, better map (cold half = -0.8) 0.02
``` ::: ::: **Two practical rules.** * **The map must not check itself.** Kriging passes through the floats it was built from, so their residuals are all $0$ and the "check" would always say the map is fine. So split the floats into two teams: team A draws the map and team B checks it, then they swap, and the two answers are averaged. * **Gaps stay the map's job.** Where no cloud reaches there are no checks, so the map's guess stands unchecked there. ## Example 4: real clouds in the toy jet The toy ocean is a meandering jet with eddies on its flanks (a Bickley jet), plus a slow drift toward warm water that makes floats pile up there. The heat content follows the streamlines: warm south, cold north. ::: {#cell-fig-velocity .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The toy's true velocity field on one day. Left: speed (grey) and streamlines of the jet and its eddies. Right: the weak drift toward warm water (arrows, about 1 km/d) over the heat-content field (faded; red warm, blue cold). Floats feel both, plus a random walk.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-velocity-output-1.png){#fig-velocity width=1309 height=407} ::: ::: Real clouds are not rectangles. The currents shape them: * in a jet a cloud is a long thin ribbon: certain to stay in the jet, but unsure how far along it; * among eddies a cloud spreads wide and can split; * in quiet water a cloud stays compact. ::: {#cell-fig-clouds .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Particle clouds from three anchors (stars) after 1, 4 and 16 ten-day cycles, over the heat-content field (faded; red warm, blue cold). Black: jet core. Green: eddy flank. Gold: quiet water.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-clouds-output-1.png){#fig-clouds width=1419 height=385} ::: ::: Now run the full recipe on one snapshot of 60 floats in the toy jet (details in [the full toy report](simex.qmd)). Each float's anchor is where it really was 4 cycles (40 days) ago. A cloud is released from each anchor, and the clouds are stacked at today's time. ::: {#cell-fig-paths .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 60 real floats over the last 4 cycles: anchors (open circles), their 10-day positions joined by straight lines, and today's profiles (orange). The clouds behind the next figure start at the open circles.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-paths-output-1.png){#fig-paths width=924 height=407} ::: ::: Floats that drifted into the warm south sit where the stacked density is high and get small weights; the few in the cold north get large ones. ::: {#cell-fig-snapshot .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: stacked density (darker = more floats expected) from the 60 clouds launched at the anchors above, with each float drawn at a size proportional to its weight; outside the black line no cloud reaches (gap). Right: each float's weight relative to an equal share, against its heat content.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-snapshot-output-1.png){#fig-snapshot width=1309 height=429} ::: ::: On this snapshot the simple average is \+0\.47, the reweighted average is \-0\.04, and the truth is \+0\.00. ## Example 5: map + check on the toy jet, start to finish The same snapshot as Example 4, run through the map + check recipe one step at a time. Every cloud here uses 1,600 particles. With only 100 particles a cloud's thin tails are full of holes, which show up as spurious gaps and occasional huge weights. The 60 floats are split into two fixed teams: **team A** (circles) and **team B** (triangles). First A draws the map and B checks it. Then they swap roles. The final answer is the average of the two. ### Direction 1: team A maps, team B checks ::: {#cell-fig-dr-story-ab .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Direction 1. 1: the truth. 2: what the floats measure. 3: where team B's floats could have been, given their positions 4 cycles earlier (black line = edge of the gap). 4: team A's kriging map. 5: the map's true error (faint background) and team B's measured residuals. 6: the same residuals with marker size proportional to their weight.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-dr-story-ab-output-1.png){#fig-dr-story-ab width=1412 height=781} ::: ::: 1. **True field.** Warm south, cold north, eddies along the jet. The box mean is \+0\.00. 2. **Observations.** The floats have piled up in the warm south, so their simple average is \+0\.47. 3. **Possible locations.** The stacked density of team B's clouds. The south is dark (many floats expected there); the cold north is pale (few expected). 4. **Team A's kriging map.** It looks like the truth where team A is dense, but it fills the sparse cold north with values that are too warm. Its box average is \+0\.42. 5. **Residuals.** Team B's measured values minus the map. In the south the map is roughly right and the residuals are small. The few northern triangles show the map is too warm there. A plain average of the residuals is only \-0\.20, because the crowded south outvotes the north. 6. **Reweighted residuals.** The 8 northern team-B floats are 27% of the team but get 53% of the weight. The weighted correction is \-0\.52, and this direction gives \+0\.42 \-0\.52 = **\-0\.11**. ### Direction 2: team B maps, team A checks ::: {#cell-fig-dr-story-ba .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Direction 2, the same six steps with the roles swapped: team B (triangles) draws the map, and team A (circles) checks it with its own clouds.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-dr-story-ba-output-1.png){#fig-dr-story-ba width=1412 height=781} ::: ::: * **Team B's map** is a different, imperfect guess: too warm in the north again, but now a little too cold in the south. Its box average is \+0\.18. * **Plain checks point the wrong way.** Most of team A sits in the south, where this map is too cold, so the plain residual average is \+0\.12. That pushes the answer *warmer*. * **Weighted checks push the right way, but only partly.** Team A has only 4 floats in the north (13% of the team). Weighting raises their share to 30%, and the correction flips to \-0\.03. One of those northern floats crossed the jet from the south in the last 4 cycles, which team A's clouds rate as very unlikely. It lands in a gap (white region in panel 3) and gets no weight. The cold north is therefore thinly represented in this direction, which gives **\+0\.16**. ### Putting it together ::: {#cell-fig-dr-summary .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![From the simple average to the final estimate on this snapshot. Grey: estimates that use no weights. Orange: each map after its weighted check (arrows), and the final average of the two directions.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-dr-summary-output-1.png){#fig-dr-summary width=984 height=385} ::: ::: ::: {#77a29aac .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
box mean
simple average of all floats 0.47
team A map 0.42
team A map + plain team B check 0.22
team A map + weighted team B check -0.11
team B map 0.18
team B map + plain team A check 0.31
team B map + weighted team A check 0.16
final: average of the two weighted directions 0.03
truth 0.00
``` ::: ::: The two maps disagree (\+0\.42 and \+0\.18), and plain checks leave both well off. After the weighted checks the two directions land on either side of the truth (\-0\.11 and \+0\.16), and their average is **\+0\.03**, against a truth of \+0\.00 and a simple average of \+0\.47. ## When it goes wrong Averaged over 40 repeats of the toy (looking back 4 cycles): ::: {#e84bf8ec .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
estimator scenario simple average kriging map weights only map + check
correct model 0.42 0.14 -0.05 0.01
model misses convergence 0.42 0.14 0.13 0.07
model eddies displaced 0.42 0.14 0.03 0.05
noise too small (K/4) 0.42 0.14 -0.10 0.06
noise too large (4K) 0.42 0.14 0.20 0.10
``` ::: ::: The simple average and the kriging map don't use the drift model, so they are the same in every row. * **Model right:** both weighted versions are close to zero. The small negative value for weights only comes from using only 100 particles per cloud and goes away with more. * **Map + check** has the smaller error in most rows, because a wrong weight now only scales the map's mistake instead of the full heat content. * **Clouds too narrow** (noise too small): a float landing just outside its own cloud looks like a rare event and gets a huge weight. * **Clouds too wide** (noise too large): every float gets about the same weight, which slides back toward the simple average. * **Model eddies in the wrong place:** a float trapped in a real warm eddy lands where the model says it shouldn't, so it is overweighted. * **Looking back too far** when the model misses some drift: the error creeps back toward the simple average. * **Looking back too little:** the clouds are small, gaps open where floats avoid, and the weights cannot reach the gaps. The [full toy report](simex.qmd) has the details.
